_note: Name-facts for the United States (FT-36, docs/PLAN_V0.8.md). See
American city names fall into a few repeating kinds, and saying which
kind a name is turns out to be the hook: a transplanted English or
Dutch name (Boston, Harlem), a Spanish saint (San Diego, San Antonio),
a native word the settlers kept (Chicago, Milwaukee), or a person
(Houston, Denver, Cleveland). Where the story is thin, the second fact
These ids are shared with usa-cities-east/-center/-west, so each
sentence is written once here and appears on all four maps.
seattle: Named for Chief Si'ahl of the Duwamish and Suquamish, who was friendly to the settlers; the city anglicised his name and he is buried across the sound from it.
Boeing, Microsoft, Amazon and Starbucks all started here.
Its Pike Place Market has run since 1907, and the city regrades of 1898–1930 washed entire hills into the bay.
portland: Decided by a coin toss in 1845: two founders wanted Boston and Portland after their home towns, and the Maine man won two throws out of three.
The losing penny survives and is on display in the city's historical society.
Powell’s City of Books fills a whole block and is the largest independent bookshop in the world.
minneapolis: Half Dakota, half Greek: mni is water in Dakota, polis is city in Greek — the water city.
It has thirteen lakes inside the city limits, which is what the name was pointing at.
Its skyway system links 80 blocks indoors, which matters in a city that reaches −30 °C.
milwaukee: From an Algonquian word usually read as "good land" or "gathering place by the river".
Germans arriving after 1848 made it the beer capital of America — Pabst, Schlitz and Miller were all brewed here.
The Harley-Davidson motorcycle was built here in a wooden shed in 1903.
buffalo: Probably a mangled French beau fleuve, "beautiful river" — there were never any buffalo here.
The Erie Canal ended at its harbour, which is why it grew, and the St Lawrence Seaway bypassing it is why it stopped.
Buffalo wings were invented at the Anchor Bar in 1964, from a part of the chicken nobody wanted.
detroit: French détroit, "the strait" — the narrow water between Lake Erie and Lake St Clair that it guards.
Ford's moving assembly line started here in 1913 and cut the time to build a car from twelve hours to ninety minutes.
Motown Records started in a house on West Grand Boulevard and recorded in its converted garage.
boston: Named for Boston in Lincolnshire, which is itself worn down from "Botolph's stone".
Its street plan follows cow paths and colonial shorelines, which is why it is the least grid-like big city in the country.
Its subway opened in 1897, the first in America, and Harvard across the river dates from 1636.
chicago: From shikaakwa, the Miami-Illinois word for the wild garlic that grew in the marshes here.
After the fire of 1871 it rebuilt with the first steel-framed skyscraper, and it reversed its river in 1900 so the sewage flowed away from the lake.
The Willis Tower held the world height record for 25 years, and the city has 26 miles of public lakefront.
providence: Roger Williams, thrown out of Massachusetts for arguing that church and state should be separate, named it for "God's merciful providence" in guiding him there.
The colony he founded was the first to guarantee freedom of religion.
Brown University is here, and the city sits at the head of Narragansett Bay on seven hills.
cleveland: Named for Moses Cleaveland, who surveyed it in 1796; a newspaper is said to have dropped the first a to fit its masthead.
Its river caught fire in 1969 — oil slick and debris — and the outrage helped produce the Clean Water Act.
The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame is here, because a local DJ coined the phrase in 1951.
bridgeport: Literally what it was: the port at the bridge over the Pequonnock.
P. T. Barnum was its mayor, and he built the circus's winter quarters here.
Connecticut’s largest city, and its Beardsley Park was laid out by Frederick Law Olmsted.

region: Named in 1664 for the Duke of York, later James II, when the English took New Amsterdam from the Dutch.
The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, linked the Hudson to the Great Lakes and made New York the busiest port in the country.
Its Adirondack Park is larger than Yellowstone, Yosemite, Grand Canyon and Glacier combined, and is constitutionally "forever wild".
city: New Amsterdam until the English took it in 1664 and renamed it for the Duke of York.
Dutch names survive all over it: Brooklyn was Breukelen, Harlem was Haarlem, and the Bronx was the farm of Jonas Bronck.
About 800 languages are spoken in it, more than anywhere else on earth, and Queens alone has some 160.

pittsburgh: For William Pitt, British prime minister, named by the general who took the fort in 1758.
It keeps the -h that most American -burgs lost, after a twenty-year fight with the federal board that had spelled it Pittsburg.
It has 446 bridges, more than any other city in the world, because three rivers meet here.
columbus: For Christopher Columbus, chosen in 1812 when naming things after him was a young republic's way of claiming a founding story.
It is the Ohio one — there are Columbuses in sixteen other states, which is why this map has to say Ohio.
Ohio State has one of the largest student bodies in the country, and the city is the state capital.
philadelphia: Greek for "brotherly love" — philos and adelphos — the name William Penn gave his Quaker colony's capital.
Penn laid it out on a grid with five squares in 1682, a century before anyone else in America thought to plan a city.
The Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were both written and signed here.
indianapolis: "Indiana" plus the Greek polis, coined in 1821 for a capital that did not exist yet.
Built on a site chosen for being the middle of the state, with no river worth using — one of the few big American cities not founded on navigable water.
Its 500-mile race has run since 1911 and fills the largest sports venue on earth, seating 250,000.
denver: For James Denver, governor of Kansas Territory — the founders were flattering a man who had already resigned without knowing it.
The Mile High City, exactly: one step on the Capitol's west stairs is 5,280 feet above sea level.
The Rockies rise straight out of the plains west of it, and the thin air makes baseballs fly further.
baltimore: For Lord Baltimore, the Irish title of the family that founded Maryland; Baltimore itself is baile an tí mhóir, "town of the big house".
The bombardment of its Fort McHenry in 1814 is what Francis Scott Key was watching when he wrote the national anthem.
Its harbour clipper ships were the fastest afloat in the 1800s, built for speed over cargo.
cincinnati: For the Society of the Cincinnati, Revolutionary officers who named themselves after Cincinnatus, the Roman who left his plough to save Rome and then went back to it.
It was called Losantiville for two years first, a made-up word meaning "town opposite the mouth of the Licking".
It was America’s first boomtown, and was called Porkopolis for the pork it packed and shipped downriver.
kansas-city: Named for the Kansa people, whose name is usually read as "people of the south wind".
There are two of them either side of the state line, and this is the bigger, in Missouri.
It claims more fountains than any city except Rome, and its barbecue is a style in its own right.
washington-d-c: George Washington chose the site but never called it after himself; Congress did that, and the District of Columbia is a Latin flourish for the same Columbus.
It is in no state on purpose: the founders did not want the capital beholden to one.
No building may rise above a limit set in 1910, which is why it stays low and the Capitol still dominates.
st-louis: For Louis IX of France, the crusading king made a saint — the city was French before it was American, and named for the patron of the king who then ruled it.
Its Gateway Arch is the tallest monument in the country, marking where the westward expansion set off.
The 1904 World’s Fair and Olympics were both held here, and the ice cream cone was popularised at them.
sacramento: For the Santísimo Sacramento — the Blessed Sacrament — the name a Spanish explorer gave the river in 1808.
The Gold Rush started 60 km away at Sutter's Mill, and the city grew as the place the miners bought their shovels.
California’s capital, built where two rivers meet, and the western end of the first transcontinental railroad.
oakland: For the coast live oaks that covered the hills when it was founded in 1852.
Gertrude Stein grew up here and wrote the line everyone quotes against it: "there is no there there" — she meant her childhood home was gone.
Its port pioneered container shipping in 1962, and it is the greenest big city in California by tree cover.
san-francisco: For St Francis of Assisi, via the Spanish mission founded in 1776.
It went from about 1,000 people to 25,000 in a year when gold was found in 1848, and ships were abandoned in the bay by crews who ran for the hills.
The 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed about 80% of it, and it was largely rebuilt within a decade.
san-jose: For St Joseph — the first Spanish civil town in California, founded 1777, before either San Francisco or Los Angeles had a village.
Now the biggest city in the Bay Area and the capital of Silicon Valley, which has no official boundaries at all.
It has more engineers per head than anywhere in America, and the Winchester house here has stairs that lead nowhere.
virginia-beach: The plainest name on this map: the beach in Virginia, which is itself named for Elizabeth I, the virgin queen.
Its 56 km of seafront are in the record books as the longest pleasure beach in the world.
The first English colonists in America landed at Cape Henry here in 1607, before moving up to Jamestown.
norfolk: For Norfolk in England — the "north folk" of East Anglia, as Suffolk were the south.
It has the largest naval base on earth, and the deep harbour is why the city is there at all.
Its harbour has never frozen, which is why the navy chose it, and the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel runs 28 km across the bay mouth.
las-vegas: Spanish for "the meadows" — there were springs and grass here, which is why a desert road stopped at this spot.
The springs ran dry in 1962; the city that grew on them now draws its water from the Colorado.
The Strip is not in the city at all — it lies just outside the limits, in unincorporated Clark County.
raleigh: For Sir Walter Raleigh, who sent the first English colonists to this coast in the 1580s and never set foot in America himself.
Like Indianapolis it was built to be a capital, chosen in 1792 for sitting near the middle of the state.
With Durham and Chapel Hill it forms the Research Triangle, named for the three universities at its corners.
memphis: For the ancient Egyptian capital on the Nile — the founders were naming a city on a great river and reached for the grandest precedent they knew.
Sun Studio here recorded Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash and Jerry Lee Lewis, and Stax made the city the home of Southern soul.
It sits on the Mississippi, and FedEx built the world’s busiest cargo airport around its runway here.
san-bernardino: For St Bernardino of Siena, named by Spanish missionaries who crossed the pass on his feast day in 1810.
Route 66's original end ran through it, and the first McDonald's opened here in 1940.
The Cajon Pass beside it is the gap through the mountains that every railway, road and pipeline to Los Angeles uses.
los-angeles: Short for El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles — the town of Our Lady the Queen of the Angels, founded 1781.
It annexed its way to size: the map is full of independent cities it grew around rather than swallowed.
It has more museums than any other American city, and the La Brea tar pits in the middle of it still bubble fossils.
long-beach: Named in 1888 for the obvious: a long, flat beach, which the developers were selling.
Its port and Los Angeles's share one harbour and together handle about a third of everything imported into the country.
The Queen Mary has been moored here as a hotel since 1967, and oil is still pumped from islands disguised as resorts.
atlanta: A railway invention: the end of the Western and Atlantic line, feminised into Atlanta.
Sherman burned it in 1864, which is why almost nothing in the centre predates the Civil War.
Its airport is the busiest in the world, and Coca-Cola was invented here in 1886 by a pharmacist.
irvine: For James Irvine, a Gold Rush merchant who bought a 400 km² ranch; the city was built on it in 1971 to a single plan.
One of the few large American cities that is entirely master-planned, village by village.
Consistently among the safest cities of its size in America, and built around a university opened in 1965.
birmingham: For Birmingham in England, because both were built on iron — the founders were declaring an ambition in 1871.
It is the only place in the world with coal, iron ore and limestone, the three things steel needs, all within a few kilometres.
A 17 m cast-iron statue of Vulcan, the largest in the world, stands over it — the god of the forge, for the iron.
phoenix: Named by a settler who saw the canals of a vanished people and said a new city would rise from their ashes — the Hohokam had irrigated this valley for a thousand years and gone.
The modern canals follow the Hohokam lines, and the city is the hottest big one in the country.
The fifth largest city in America, and the largest state capital, spread over 1,340 km² of desert.
mesa: Spanish for "table" — the flat-topped plateau the town was laid out on in 1878.
Bigger than Atlanta, Miami or St Louis, and almost nobody outside Arizona has heard of it.
It has more spring-training baseball history than anywhere, and the Superstition Mountains rise right behind it.
dallas: Nobody is sure which Dallas: most likely George Dallas, vice-president in the 1840s, but the founder never wrote it down.
It has no natural reason to be there — no port, no pass, no mine — and grew because railways crossed at that spot.
The integrated circuit was invented here at Texas Instruments in 1958, which started the whole computer age.
fort-worth: An actual fort, built in 1849 and named for General William Worth of the Mexican War.
It calls itself "where the West begins", and the cattle drives up the Chisholm Trail are why.
Its stockyards still drive a longhorn cattle herd down the street twice a day, and the Kimbell museum is a Louis Kahn masterpiece.
san-diego: For San Diego de Alcalá, named on his feast day in 1602 — and the site of the first Spanish mission in California, in 1769.
Its bay is the best natural harbour on the coast, which is why the Pacific Fleet lives there.
Its zoo pioneered open enclosures without bars, and the city has the mildest big-city climate in America.
austin: For Stephen F. Austin, who brought the first American settlers into what was then Mexican Texas.
The state capital, and the only big Texan city people describe as green and hilly — it sits on the edge of the Hill Country.
A million and a half bats live under the Congress Avenue bridge and fly out at dusk all summer.
houston: For Sam Houston, who won Texas its independence at San Jacinto and then served as president of the Republic.
It has no zoning code, which is why a refinery, a cathedral and a taquería can share a block.
Mission Control is here, which is why the first word spoken from the Moon was "Houston".
san-antonio: For St Anthony of Padua, named on his feast day in 1691 by a Spanish expedition camped by the river.
The Alamo was one of its five Spanish missions before it was a battlefield.
Its River Walk runs a storey below the streets, built in the 1930s as flood control and now the city’s centre.
orlando: Probably for a soldier named Orlando Reeves who died here in 1835, though the records are thin enough that the town may have invented him.
Disney bought 110 km² of swamp through shell companies in the 1960s so nobody would raise the price.
More people visit it each year than any other American city, and it has more hotel rooms than anywhere except Las Vegas.
tampa: A Calusa word recorded by the Spanish, meaning something like "sticks of fire" — possibly for the lightning, which is the worst in the country here.
Cuban cigar makers built Ybor City here in the 1880s, and José Martí planned the Cuban revolution from its rolling floors.
Its port is Florida’s largest, and the Gasparilla pirate festival has been held since 1904.
west-palm-beach: West of Palm Beach, which is named for coconut palms that grew from a Spanish ship wrecked in 1878 with 20,000 coconuts aboard.
Henry Flagler built it as the place his hotel's staff lived, across the water from the guests.
The Norton Museum here holds one of the best Chinese collections in America, endowed by a steel magnate.
fort-lauderdale: Forts built in the Second Seminole War, named for Major William Lauderdale who commanded the men who built them.
It has 300 km of canals, which is why it is called the Venice of America.
More than 45,000 boats are registered here, and it hosts the largest boat show in the world.
miami: From Mayaimi, the name of a lake and the people beside it — a Native word, not a Spanish one, despite the city's Spanish present.
It was incorporated in 1896 by 344 voters, a third of them Black Bahamians, and it is the only major American city founded by a woman — Julia Tuttle.
More than half its residents were born abroad — a higher share than any other large American city.
north-dakota: Dakota is the Sioux word for "friend" or "ally" — the people’s own name for themselves.
It was split from South Dakota in 1889, and the two were admitted on the same day with the papers shuffled so nobody knows which was 39th and which 40th.
The Bakken shale under it made it briefly the second-largest oil producer in the country, and its population grew after a century of decline.
washington: The only state named after a president — and it was nearly called Columbia, changed to avoid confusion with the District of Columbia.
That change failed entirely: people say Washington State to this day to avoid exactly that confusion.
Mount St Helens here lost 400 m of its summit in 1980 in the deadliest eruption in US history.
montana: From Spanish montaña, "mountain" — chosen by a congressman who liked the sound of it.
The fourth largest state with the third lowest population density; it has more cattle than people.
Custer was killed at the Little Bighorn here in 1876, and Glacier National Park has lost most of the glaciers it was named for.
minnesota: From Dakota mni sota, "sky-tinted water" or "cloudy water", for the Minnesota river.
It calls itself the land of 10,000 lakes and actually has about 11,842.
The Mississippi rises here at Lake Itasca, narrow enough to step across.
idaho: A made-up word: a lobbyist claimed it was Shoshone for "gem of the mountains", then admitted he had invented it — but the name had stuck.
It grows about a third of all US potatoes, in volcanic soil watered by the Snake River.
Hells Canyon on its border is the deepest river gorge in North America, deeper than the Grand Canyon.
maine: Probably from the French province of Maine, or simply from "the main" — sailors’ shorthand for the mainland as against the islands.
The most forested state, about 89% trees, and it produces nearly all the wild blueberries in the country.
Its coastline is 5,600 km once the inlets are counted, longer than California’s.
michigan: From Ojibwe mishigami, "large water" — for the lake.
The only state in two separate pieces, joined by a five-mile bridge over the Straits of Mackinac.
It touches four of the five Great Lakes, and no point in it is more than 137 km from one.
wisconsin: From a Miami word recorded by the French as Meskousing, probably "river running through a red place"; the spelling drifted to Wisconsin.
It makes about a quarter of all American cheese, and its residents are called cheeseheads without embarrassment.
The Republican Party was founded in Ripon here in 1854, and the state pioneered workers’ compensation and unemployment insurance.
south-dakota: The same Dakota — "friend" in Sioux — as its northern twin.
Mount Rushmore was carved between 1927 and 1941 into a mountain sacred to the Lakota, whose claim to the Black Hills the Supreme Court upheld in 1980.
They refused the compensation, which now sits accruing interest at over a billion dollars, because accepting it would confirm the sale.
oregon: Origin genuinely unknown: possibly from a French map’s mislabelled "Ouaricon-sint", or from a Spanish or Algonquian word.
Crater Lake here is the deepest lake in the United States at 594 m, filling the caldera of a collapsed volcano.
It has no sales tax, and by law you could not pump your own petrol in most of the state until 2023.
new-hampshire: Named in 1629 after the English county of Hampshire by a captain who had lived there.
Its presidential primary has gone first in the nation since 1920, which is written into state law.
The Old Man of the Mountain, its stone-face emblem, collapsed in 2003 — the state kept it on the licence plates.
vermont: From French vert mont, "green mountain" — the name of the Green Mountain Boys who fought for its independence.
It was an independent republic from 1777 to 1791, with its own currency and postal service.
The first state to abolish adult slavery in its constitution, in 1777, and it has no billboards by law.
wyoming: From a Delaware phrase, xwé:wamənk, "at the big river flat" — a Pennsylvania valley name transplanted 2,000 km west.
The least populous state, with fewer people than several American cities.
It gave women the vote in 1869, half a century before the nation, and Yellowstone here was the world’s first national park.
massachusetts: From the Massachusett people: "at the great hill", probably the Blue Hills near Boston.
Harvard, founded 1636, is the oldest university in the country, and the first American public school and first subway are both here.
It was the first state to legalise same-sex marriage, in 2004.
iowa: Named for the Ioway people, whose own name may come from a word meaning "sleepy ones" given by neighbours.
It has about a quarter of the best-grade farmland in the country and grows more corn than any other state.
Its caucuses opened the presidential nominating season for half a century.
rhode-island: Probably from Dutch roodt eylandt, "red island", for its clay — or from a supposed likeness to Rhodes.
The smallest state, and the one with the longest official name: it was "the State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations" until 2020.
It was founded by Roger Williams as a refuge for religious dissenters, and had the first Baptist church and the oldest synagogue in America.
connecticut: From Mohegan quinnitukqut, "at the long tidal river".
Its 1639 Fundamental Orders are sometimes called the first written constitution in the Western world, which is why it is the Constitution State.
Hartford has been the insurance capital of America since the 1800s, starting with fire policies.
nebraska: From Otoe ñí braðke or Omaha ni btháska, "flat water" — the Platte river, which is exactly that.
The only state with a unicameral, officially nonpartisan legislature.
Its Sandhills are the largest sand dune area in the Western Hemisphere, held in place by grass.
pennsylvania: "Penn’s woods" — but named for William Penn’s father; Penn himself was embarrassed and tried to have it changed.
The Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were both signed in Philadelphia.
It is officially a Commonwealth, as are Virginia, Massachusetts and Kentucky, which means nothing legally.
ohio: From Seneca ohi:yo’, "good river" or "large creek".
Eight presidents were born here, more than any state except Virginia, which is why it is called the Mother of Presidents.
The Wright brothers were from Dayton, and both Neil Armstrong and John Glenn were Ohioans.
new-jersey: Named for the Channel Island of Jersey, home of one of the colony’s proprietors.
The most densely populated state, and it has more diners than anywhere else in the country.
Edison’s Menlo Park lab here produced the phonograph and the practical light bulb, and the first baseball game was played in Hoboken.
indiana: "Land of the Indians", coined for a land company in 1768 — a name given by settlers, not by the people it names.
Its 500-mile race has run at the Brickyard since 1911.
It has more miles of interstate per square mile than any other state, which is why it calls itself the Crossroads of America.
illinois: From the Illinois Confederation, through French — the -ois ending is a French spelling, which is why the s is silent.
Chicago’s 1871 fire led to the rebuilding that produced the world’s first skyscraper in 1885.
It produces more soybeans and nuclear power than any other state.
utah: From the Ute people; the name may mean "people of the mountains".
The Great Salt Lake in it is the largest lake west of the Mississippi and saltier than the ocean.
About 62% of its people are Mormon, and Salt Lake City was founded in 1847 by settlers who walked there.
delaware: Named for the Delaware river, itself named for Lord De La Warr, a colonial governor — the Lenape people were then renamed after him too.
The first state to ratify the Constitution, in 1787, which is why it is called the First State.
More than half of all US public companies are legally incorporated here, for its courts and its corporate law.
colorado: Spanish for "coloured red", for the silt in the Colorado river.
It has more land above 3,000 m than any other state, and its lowest point is higher than the highest point in eighteen others.
Its border is drawn entirely with straight lines, though survey errors left it with 697 sides rather than four.
west-virginia: It split from Virginia in 1863 rather than leave the Union — the only state formed by seceding from a seceding state.
Almost entirely mountainous, with the highest average elevation east of the Mississippi.
The Hatfield-McCoy feud ran along its Kentucky border, and coal mining shaped both its economy and its politics.
district-of-columbia: Columbia is a poetic name for America, from Columbus; the district was carved from Maryland and Virginia to belong to no state.
Its residents had no presidential vote until 1961 and still have no voting member of Congress — hence the licence plates reading "taxation without representation".
No building may rise above a 1910 height limit, which is why the city stays low and the Capitol still dominates.
maryland: For Henrietta Maria, queen of Charles I — one of several colonies named for a monarch’s wife.
The Star-Spangled Banner was written here during the 1814 bombardment of Fort McHenry.
The Chesapeake Bay in it is the largest estuary in the country, and its blue crabs are a state institution.
nevada: Spanish for "snow-covered", from the Sierra Nevada on its western edge — which is odd for the driest state in the country.
The federal government owns about 80% of it, more than any other state.
Gambling was legalised in 1931 during the Depression, and the Hoover Dam was built the same decade.
kansas: From the Kansa people, whose name means "people of the south wind".
It is measurably flatter than a pancake, by an actual study that compared both.
Its 1954 Brown v. Board of Education case ended legal school segregation across the country.
missouri: From a Siouan word meaning "those who have dugout canoes", the name Illinois people used for their neighbours.
The Gateway Arch in St Louis marks where westward expansion began; the Oregon, Santa Fe and California trails all started in this state.
The 1857 Dred Scott case that helped precipitate the Civil War was filed in St Louis.
virginia: For Elizabeth I, the Virgin Queen — the oldest English place name in America, given in 1584.
Eight presidents were born here, more than any other state, and four of the first five.
Jamestown in 1607 was the first permanent English settlement, and the Civil War ended at Appomattox in this state.
kentucky: From an Iroquoian word, probably kentá:ke, "on the meadow" — not, as often claimed, "dark and bloody ground".
Mammoth Cave here is the longest cave system in the world, with over 680 km mapped and no end found.
It makes about 95% of the world’s bourbon, which must by law be aged in new charred oak.
california: From a fictional island in a 1510 Spanish romance, ruled by a black queen called Calafia — explorers thought the peninsula was that island.
If it were a country it would have one of the largest economies in the world.
It holds both the highest and lowest points in the contiguous states, Mount Whitney and Death Valley, 135 km apart.
tennessee: From Tanasi, a Cherokee town on the Little Tennessee river; the meaning is not known.
It borders eight states, tied with Missouri for the most.
Memphis and Nashville between them produced blues, rock and roll and country; Sun Studio recorded Elvis, Cash and Presley’s first single.
oklahoma: From Choctaw okla humma, "red people" — proposed by a Choctaw chief for the Indian Territory.
Sixty-seven tribes were relocated here, many along the Trail of Tears, and it has the second-largest Native American population.
The 1889 land runs opened it to settlers who raced for claims; those who slipped in early were called Sooners.
north-carolina: Carolina is from Carolus, Latin for Charles — for Charles I, and later confirmed for Charles II.
The Wright brothers flew at Kitty Hawk here in 1903, choosing it for the steady wind and soft sand.
Its Outer Banks are barrier islands that shift, and the graveyard of the Atlantic offshore has wrecked over a thousand ships.
arkansas: From a French rendering of a Quapaw name — which is why it is pronounced like Kansas’s neighbour but spelled with a silent s.
The Crater of Diamonds here is the only diamond mine in the world where the public may dig and keep what they find.
Walmart was founded in Bentonville in 1962 and is now the largest company in the world by revenue.
arizona: Probably from O’odham alĩ ṣon-ak, "small spring", through Spanish Arizonac.
The Grand Canyon is 446 km long and up to 1,857 m deep, cut by the Colorado over millions of years.
It does not observe daylight saving time, except on the Navajo Nation, which does.
new-mexico: Named by Spaniards in the 1560s, decades before there was a country called Mexico — so it is not "new" anything.
The first atomic bomb was detonated at Trinity here in July 1945, and Los Alamos designed it.
It has the highest share of Hispanic residents of any state, and Santa Fe is the oldest capital city in the country, from 1610.
south-carolina: The other half of Carolus, split from the north in 1712.
The Civil War began here when Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour in April 1861.
Its Gullah communities on the Sea Islands kept a creole language and West African traditions more intact than anywhere else in the country.
georgia: For George II, who chartered it in 1732 as a colony for debtors and a buffer against Spanish Florida.
The largest state east of the Mississippi.
Martin Luther King was born in Atlanta, and the state produces most of America’s peanuts and pecans.
alabama: From the Alabama people, whose name may mean "clearers of the thicket".
The Montgomery bus boycott began here in 1955 and the Selma marches in 1965; the state is where the civil rights movement was decided.
Rockets for the Apollo programme were designed at Huntsville, which is why it is called Rocket City.
mississippi: The Delta here produced the blues, and Muddy Waters, B.B. King and Robert Johnson all came from within a hundred miles of each other.
Elvis Presley was born in Tupelo, and the state’s catfish farms supply most of the American crop.
texas: From Caddo táysha’, "friend" or "ally", which the Spanish heard as tejas — the state motto is simply "Friendship".
It was an independent republic from 1836 to 1845, and it is the only state that may legally fly its flag at the same height as the national one.
The second largest state, and its economy alone would be among the ten largest countries in the world.
louisiana: For Louis XIV, named by La Salle when he claimed the whole Mississippi basin for France in 1682.
The only state whose law derives from the Napoleonic Code rather than English common law, so it has parishes rather than counties.
The United States bought it from Napoleon in 1803 for about four cents a hectare, doubling the size of the country.
florida: Spanish for "flowery", named by Ponce de León in 1513 — probably for Pascua Florida, the Easter season, as much as for the vegetation.
The Everglades are a river 100 km wide and 15 cm deep, flowing so slowly it looks like a swamp.
It has the longest coastline in the contiguous states, and more golf courses than any other.
st-paul: It was Pig’s Eye, after a one-eyed bootlegger, until a priest built a chapel to St Paul in 1841 and the name was quietly upgraded.
It is the capital of Minnesota and the twin of Minneapolis across the Mississippi.
F. Scott Fitzgerald was born here and set some of his early stories in its Summit Avenue, the longest Victorian street in America.
lakeville: Named for the lakes around it, of which Minnesota has about 11,842.
One of the fastest-growing suburbs of the Twin Cities.
Its Airlake industrial park grew around a small airfield built in the 1940s.
appleton: Named for Samantha Appleton, whose father endowed the local college as a wedding gift.
It was the first city in the world lit by a hydroelectric central station, in 1882.
Harry Houdini grew up here and called it his home town, though he was born in Budapest.
madison: Named for James Madison, who had died three weeks before the site was chosen in 1836.
It is built on an isthmus between two lakes, with the capitol at one end and the university at the other.
Its capitol dome is the only granite one in the United States, and state law long kept any building from rising above it.
waukesha: From a Potawatomi word, probably for a fox.
It was a spa town in the 1800s, selling its spring water across the country as a cure.
A speculator tried to pipe that water to the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair and armed residents stopped him.
rockford: Named for a rocky ford across the Rock River.
It made furniture, then machine tools, and calls itself the forest city for its trees.
The Rockford Peaches of the women’s baseball league inspired the film A League of Their Own.
evanston: Named for John Evans, a founder of Northwestern University, which is the town’s centre.
The Woman’s Christian Temperance Union was founded here, and the town was dry until 1972.
The ice cream sundae is one of several inventions claimed by the town, supposedly to get round a Sunday soda ban.
elgin: Named after a Scottish hymn tune, not the town — its founder liked the melody.
The Elgin National Watch Company made about half of all American pocket watches.
Its observatory kept time for the railways, and the town set its clocks by the stars.
aurora: Named for the Roman goddess of dawn.
It was the first American city to light its entire street system electrically, in 1881, and calls itself the City of Lights.
It is the second largest city in Illinois.
gary: Named for Elbert Gary, the founding chairman of US Steel, which built the town in 1906.
The steelworks here was the largest in the world for decades.
The Jackson family lived in a small house on Jackson Street, and Michael Jackson was born in it.
des-moines: From French Rivière des Moines, probably from a Native name the French heard as "moingoana", later reinterpreted as "of the monks".
Its capitol has five domes, the central one covered in 23-carat gold leaf.
The Iowa caucuses made it the first stop of the American presidential race for half a century.
davenport: Named for George Davenport, an English-born trader who was later murdered in his own house on the Fourth of July.
It is one of the Quad Cities on the Mississippi, and one of the few river cities with no flood wall — it uses parkland instead.
Bix Beiderbecke, the cornet player, was born here.
joliet: Named for Louis Jolliet, the French explorer who passed through in 1673 — with a letter dropped.
Its limestone quarries built much of Chicago, and its prison, opened 1858, appears in The Blues Brothers.
A stretch of Route 66 runs through the town.
omaha: From the Omaha people, whose name means roughly "those going against the current".
It was the starting point of the first transcontinental railroad in 1863.
Warren Buffett has lived in the same house here since 1958, which is why he is called the Oracle of Omaha.
lincoln: Renamed from Lancaster in 1867 for the assassinated president — by opponents of the move, who hoped the name would sink it.
It is the capital of Nebraska, and its capitol is a 122 m tower rather than a dome.
The state legislature that sits in it is the only unicameral, officially nonpartisan one in the country.
kansas-city-kansas: The smaller of the two Kansas Cities, on the Kansas side of the state line.
It grew around stockyards and meatpacking, and its Strawberry Hill district was settled by Croatians and Slovaks.
The two cities share a metropolitan area split down the middle by a state border.
kansas-city-missouri: The larger Kansas City, in Missouri — both take their name from the Kansa people.
It claims more fountains than any city except Rome.
Its barbecue is a style in its own right, and Charlie Parker grew up in its jazz district at 18th and Vine.
columbia: From Columbia, the poetic name for America derived from Columbus.
It is the home of the University of Missouri, which founded the first journalism school in the world in 1908.
The town is regularly ranked among the best small American cities to live in.
st-charles: Named for St Charles Borromeo; it was Les Petites Côtes, "the little hills", under the French.
It was Missouri’s first state capital, and Lewis and Clark set off from here in 1804.
Its Main Street is one of the longest preserved colonial-era streets in the country.
wichita: From the Wichita people, whose own name for themselves is Kitikiti’sh.
Cessna, Beechcraft and Learjet were all founded here, which is why it is called the Air Capital of the World.
Pizza Hut and White Castle both started in the city.
springfield: One of the commonest place names in America — this is Illinois’s capital, named for a spring by a field.
Lincoln lived here for 24 years, and it holds his home, his law office and his tomb.
The horseshoe sandwich, an open sandwich buried in chips and cheese sauce, was invented in the town.
tulsa: From Creek tallasi, "old town" — the name the Muscogee brought with them on the Trail of Tears.
Oil made it the Oil Capital of the World in the 1920s, which is why it has so much art deco.
The 1921 Tulsa race massacre destroyed the Greenwood district, then one of the wealthiest Black communities in America.
oklahoma-city: Named for the territory: Choctaw okla humma, "red people".
It was founded in a single afternoon on 22 April 1889, when about 10,000 people raced for plots in a land run.
The 1995 bombing of its federal building killed 168 people; a memorial with 168 empty chairs stands on the site.
bartlett: Named for Gabriel Bartlett, an early settler — this is the Tennessee one, near Memphis.
It was called Union Depot before the railway named it for him.
It is one of the larger suburbs of Memphis.
little-rock: From la petite roche, a small rock outcrop on the Arkansas River that French explorers used as a landmark.
A larger outcrop upstream was la grande roche, which is why the small one got the name.
The 1957 desegregation of its Central High School, enforced by federal troops, was a turning point in the civil rights movement.
lubbock: Named for Thomas Lubbock, a Confederate colonel and brother of a Texas governor.
It is the centre of the largest contiguous cotton-growing region in the world.
Buddy Holly was born here, and the plane crash that killed him is commemorated in the town.
arlington: Named after Arlington, Virginia, the site of Robert E. Lee’s estate.
It is the largest American city with no public transport system of any kind for most of its history.
It holds Six Flags Over Texas and the stadiums of both the Cowboys and the Rangers.
shreveport: Named for Henry Shreve, who cleared a 290 km logjam on the Red River that had blocked it for centuries.
That Great Raft took him and his successors decades to remove.
It was the capital of Confederate Louisiana and the last Confederate capital to surrender.
jackson: Named for Andrew Jackson, and the capital of Mississippi.
Sherman burned so much of it in 1863 that it was nicknamed Chimneyville.
Eudora Welty lived in the same house here for 76 years, and it is preserved as she left it.
mobile: From the Mauvila people, whose name the French wrote as Mobile.
The first Mardi Gras in America was celebrated here in 1703, fifteen years before New Orleans existed.
It was the capital of French Louisiana before New Orleans took over.
baton-rouge: French for "red stick" — a reddened cypress pole marking a boundary between two peoples, seen by explorers in 1699.
Its capitol, built by Huey Long in 1932, is the tallest in the United States at 137 m.
Long was shot in its corridor three years later.
pensacola: From the Pensacola people, whose name is thought to mean "hair people".
A Spanish settlement here in 1559 predates St Augustine, but a hurricane destroyed it and it was abandoned.
It has flown five flags — Spanish, French, British, Confederate and American — and is home to the Blue Angels.
metairie: From French métairie, a tenant farm worked for a share of the crop.
It is the largest community in Louisiana without a city government of its own.
Its cemetery was built on a racetrack, which is why its paths curve in an oval.
new-orleans: Named for the Duke of Orléans, regent of France when it was founded in 1718.
Jazz was born here, and the city is built mostly below sea level behind levees.
Hurricane Katrina flooded about 80% of it in 2005 after those levees failed.
pasadena: From a Chippewa word meaning "valley" — this is the Texas one, near Houston, named after the Californian city.
It is dominated by petrochemical refineries along the ship channel.
Gilley’s, the club in Urban Cowboy, was here, with its mechanical bull.
corpus-christi: "Body of Christ" — the bay was found on that feast day in 1519.
It is the birthplace of Selena, and a memorial to her stands on the bayfront.
Its port is one of the largest in the United States by tonnage, largely from crude oil exports.
laredo: Named for Laredo in Spain, itself possibly from a Basque word for a pasture.
It was the capital of the short-lived Republic of the Rio Grande in 1840.
It is the largest inland port in the United States, handling most trade with Mexico by truck.
mcallen: Named for John McAllen, a Scottish-born rancher who donated land for the railway.
It is one of the busiest border crossings and a major birdwatching destination.
More species have been recorded in its Rio Grande valley than almost anywhere else in the country.
rochester: Named for Nathaniel Rochester, who bought the land in 1803 — this is the New York one.
Kodak, Xerox and Bausch & Lomb were all founded here, making it a capital of imaging.
Susan B. Anthony was arrested in the city in 1872 for voting, and Frederick Douglass published his newspaper there.
syracuse: Named for Syracuse in Sicily, because the salt springs nearby reminded a visitor of a lake there.
It supplied most of the salt in the United States in the 1800s and was called Salt City.
The Erie Canal ran straight through its main street, which is now a road.
flint: Named for the Flint River, itself a translation of an Ojibwe name for its stony bed.
General Motors was founded here in 1908, and the 1936-37 sit-down strike created the modern American labour movement.
The 2014 switch of its water supply caused a lead-poisoning crisis that made the city a national scandal.
grand-rapids: Named for the rapids on the Grand River, which were later flattened by dams.
It made so much furniture that it was called Furniture City, and it was the first American city to fluoridate its water, in 1945.
Gerald Ford grew up here and is buried on his museum’s grounds.
lansing: Named after Lansing, New York, which was itself named for a lawyer who vanished in 1829 and was never found.
It is the capital of Michigan, chosen in 1847 partly because it was remote enough to be safe from British Canada.
Oldsmobile was founded here, and Malcolm X spent part of his childhood in the city.
albany: Named for the Duke of York and Albany, later James II — Albany being his Scottish title.
It is one of the oldest continuously chartered cities in the United States, from 1686.
The Erie Canal ended here, which made New York the country’s main port.
lowell: Named for Francis Cabot Lowell, who memorised British power-loom designs on a visit and reproduced them.
It was America’s first large planned industrial city, staffed by young women from New England farms.
Jack Kerouac was born here and is buried in the town.
salem: From Hebrew shalom, peace — this is the Oregon capital, named by missionaries.
The Oregon Trail ended in its valley, which is why the state’s settlement began there.
Its capitol is topped not by a dome but by a gilded pioneer with an axe.
ann-arbor: Named for the wives of two founders, both called Ann, and for the burr oak groves — "Ann’s arbour".
The University of Michigan moved here in 1837 and dominates the town.
Its stadium holds over 107,000 people, the largest in the United States.
worcester: The birth control pill, the monkey wrench and the smiley face were all developed here.
The first National Woman’s Rights Convention met in the town in 1850.
hartford: Named for Hertford in England, the birthplace of a settler.
It has been the insurance capital of America since the 1800s, starting with fire policies.
Mark Twain built a house here and wrote Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn in it.
south-bend: Named for the southernmost bend of the St Joseph River.
The University of Notre Dame was founded here in 1842 by French priests.
Studebaker built wagons and then cars in the town for over a century.
toledo: Named for Toledo in Spain, apparently chosen simply because it was easy to say.
Ohio and Michigan nearly went to war over it in 1835; Ohio got the city and Michigan got the Upper Peninsula.
It made so much glass that it is called the Glass City.
new-haven: Simply a new harbour, named by Puritan settlers in 1638.
Yale moved here in 1716, and the town was laid out on nine squares, one of the first planned grids in America.
The hamburger, the lollipop and the modern pizza crust are all claimed by the town, with varying evidence.
youngstown: Named for John Young, who bought the land in 1797.
Its steel mills closed almost overnight in 1977, on a day the town still calls Black Monday.
About 50,000 jobs went within a few years, and the population has fallen by more than half since.
fort-wayne: Named for General Anthony Wayne, who built a fort here in 1794.
The first night baseball game under electric light was played in the town in 1883.
It sits where three rivers meet and was a key portage between the Great Lakes and the Mississippi.
akron: From Greek akron, "summit" — it is the high point of the Ohio and Erie Canal.
Goodyear, Firestone and General Tire were all founded here, making it the Rubber Capital of the World.
Alcoholics Anonymous was founded in the town in 1935.
stamford: Named for Stamford in Lincolnshire, England.
It has more corporate headquarters per head than almost any American city, many relocated from New York.
The Hope Street area was once the centre of American lock manufacturing.
canton: Named after Canton in China, by a surveyor honouring a merchant who traded there.
The Pro Football Hall of Fame is here because the NFL was founded in a car showroom in the town in 1920.
President McKinley ran his 1896 campaign from his front porch here and is buried in the city.
newark: Named for Newark-on-Trent in England, or possibly meant as "New Ark" by its Puritan founders.
It is one of the oldest American cities, founded 1666, and its airport was the first major one in the country.
Its 1967 riots were among the most destructive of that decade and reshaped the city.
allentown: Named for William Allen, a Philadelphia mayor who founded it in 1762.
The Liberty Bell was hidden under a church floor here in 1777 to keep it from the British.
Billy Joel’s song about it was actually about Bethlehem next door; he used Allentown because it scanned.
harrisburg: Named for John Harris, who ran a ferry across the Susquehanna.
It is the capital of Pennsylvania, and its capitol was called a palace of art by Theodore Roosevelt.
Three Mile Island, the site of America’s worst nuclear accident in 1979, is a few miles downstream.
trenton: Named for William Trent, an early landowner — Trent’s town.
Washington crossed the Delaware to attack it on Christmas night 1776, the victory that saved the Revolution.
Its bridge carries the slogan "Trenton Makes, The World Takes", from its manufacturing years.
lancaster: Named for Lancaster in England — this is the Pennsylvania one.
It was the capital of the United States for one day, 27 September 1777, as Congress fled Philadelphia.
The surrounding county has one of the largest Amish populations in the world.
columbus-ohio: Named for Christopher Columbus in 1812 — it was created from nothing purely to be the state capital.
Ohio State has one of the largest student bodies in the country.
It is the largest city in Ohio and one of the fastest-growing in the Midwest.
york: Named for York in England — this is the Pennsylvania one.
The Articles of Confederation were adopted here in 1777 while Congress sheltered from the British.
It has made peppermint patties, barbells and motorcycles, and the Harley-Davidson plant here builds most of their big bikes.
dayton: Named for Jonathan Dayton, the youngest man to sign the Constitution, who never visited.
The Wright brothers had their bicycle shop here and designed the first aeroplane in it.
The 1995 agreement that ended the Bosnian war was negotiated at its air force base.
covington: Named for General Leonard Covington, killed in the War of 1812.
It faces Cincinnati across the Ohio River, joined by a suspension bridge Roebling built as a trial run for Brooklyn.
That bridge was the longest in the world when it opened in 1866.
louisville: Named for Louis XVI, in gratitude for French help in the Revolution.
The Kentucky Derby has run at Churchill Downs here since 1875, the oldest continuously held sporting event in the country.
Muhammad Ali was born here, and the Louisville Slugger bat has been made in the city since 1884.
lexington: Named for Lexington, Massachusetts, where the Revolution’s first shots were fired.
It calls itself the horse capital of the world, surrounded by thoroughbred farms on limestone pasture.
That limestone is why the grass looks blue in spring and the region is called the Bluegrass.
richmond: Named for Richmond upon Thames in England, which a founder thought the river view resembled.
It was the capital of the Confederacy and burned as it fell in 1865.
Patrick Henry gave the "give me liberty or give me death" speech in one of its churches in 1775.
hampton: Named for the Earl of Southampton — the oldest continuously English-speaking settlement in America, from 1610.
The first Africans brought to English North America landed nearby at Point Comfort in 1619.
NASA Langley here trained the Mercury astronauts and employed the mathematicians of Hidden Figures.
nashville: Named for Francis Nash, a general killed in the Revolution.
It is the capital of country music, and the Grand Ole Opry has broadcast since 1925.
It has a full-size concrete replica of the Parthenon, built for an exposition in 1897.
winston-salem: Two towns joined in 1913: Salem was founded by Moravians in 1766, Winston named for a Revolutionary officer.
R. J. Reynolds built its tobacco industry here, and the town made Camel cigarettes.
Old Salem is preserved as a working eighteenth-century Moravian village.
greensboro: Named for Nathanael Greene, whose 1781 battle here wore down Cornwallis before Yorktown.
The 1960 Woolworth’s sit-in by four students started the lunch-counter movement across the South.
That counter is now in the Smithsonian, and the building is a civil rights museum.
durham: Named for Bartlett Durham, who donated land for the railway station.
Its tobacco wealth built Duke University, and its Black Wall Street on Parrish Street was a centre of Black business.
With Raleigh and Chapel Hill it forms the Research Triangle.
knoxville: Named for Henry Knox, Washington’s secretary of war.
The 1982 World’s Fair was held here, and its gold Sunsphere still stands.
The Oak Ridge site nearby enriched the uranium for the Hiroshima bomb, in a town built in secret for 75,000 people.
charlotte: Named for Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, George III’s queen — which is why it is called the Queen City.
It is the second largest banking centre in the United States after New York.
America’s first gold rush happened nearby in 1799, when a boy found a 17-pound nugget and the family used it as a doorstop.
chattanooga: From a Creek word, possibly "rock rising to a point", for Lookout Mountain.
It was a crucial railway junction in the Civil War and was fought over repeatedly.
It was the first American city to offer citywide gigabit internet, in 2010, through its own utility.
fayetteville: Named for the Marquis de Lafayette — the first American city named for him, and the only one he visited.
Fort Bragg beside it is one of the largest military bases in the world by population.
The town was the site of North Carolina’s ratification of the Constitution in 1789.
greenville: Named for Nathanael Greene, like Greensboro — this is the South Carolina one.
Its Falls Park has a curved suspension bridge built over a waterfall that a road bridge had hidden for decades.
The textile mills here made it the Textile Capital of the World, and BMW now builds cars nearby.
huntsville: Named for John Hunt, who settled at a big spring in 1805.
Wernher von Braun and his team designed the Saturn V here, which is why it is called Rocket City.
Its Space and Rocket Center holds the largest collection of rocketry hardware in the world.
augusta: Named for Princess Augusta, mother of George III.
The Masters has been played at Augusta National since 1934.
James Brown grew up here, and a statue of him stands on Broad Street.
charleston: Named for Charles II — it was Charles Town until 1783.
The Civil War began in its harbour when Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861.
About 40% of enslaved Africans brought to North America arrived through this port.
columbus-georgia: Named for Columbus, like the Ohio city, and founded in 1828 at the head of navigation on the Chattahoochee.
Coca-Cola’s inventor, John Pemberton, developed an early version of the formula here before moving to Atlanta.
Its whitewater course on the river is the longest urban one in the world.
tallahassee: From a Muscogee word meaning "old fields" or "abandoned town".
It was chosen as Florida’s capital in 1824 because it was halfway between St Augustine and Pensacola.
It was the only Confederate capital east of the Mississippi not captured during the war.
jacksonville: Named for Andrew Jackson, the first military governor of Florida, who never visited it.
It is the largest city in the contiguous United States by land area, after a 1968 merger with its county.
Its port and naval bases make it one of the largest military centres in the country.
daytona-beach: Named for Mathias Day, who bought the land in 1870.
Its hard-packed sand beach was used for land speed records from 1903 to 1935.
That is why NASCAR was founded here, and the Daytona 500 is its biggest race.
sanford: Named for Henry Sanford, an American diplomat who founded it in 1870.
It calls itself the celery capital, having grown much of the country’s crop.
Its lake is the head of navigation on the St Johns, one of the few American rivers that flows north.
kissimmee: From a Calusa or Creek word of uncertain meaning, possibly "long water".
It was a cattle town before Walt Disney World opened next door in 1971.
Florida’s cattle industry is the oldest in the United States, started by the Spanish in the 1500s.
melbourne: Named for Melbourne, Australia — its first postmaster had lived there.
It sits on the Space Coast, and Cape Canaveral launches are visible from its beaches.
Its Indian River Lagoon is one of the most biologically diverse estuaries in North America.
st-petersburg: Named for St Petersburg in Russia, the birthplace of a co-founder who won the naming in a coin toss.
The loser got to name the hotel, and called it the Detroit.
It holds the largest collection of Salvador Dalí’s work outside Spain, and averages 361 sunny days a year.
fort-pierce: Named for a fort built in 1838 during the Second Seminole War.
Zora Neale Hurston spent her last years here and is buried in the town.
It sits on the Indian River Lagoon and is a centre of citrus growing.
sarasota: Of uncertain origin, possibly from a Spanish or Calusa name.
The Ringling circus wintered here from 1927, and John Ringling left the city an art museum and a Venetian Gothic mansion.
Siesta Key beach is almost pure quartz, which is why the sand stays cool underfoot.
coral-springs: Named by a development company for coral rock and a spring, neither of which is actually there.
It was planned from scratch in 1963 with strict rules on architecture and signage.
No building may have a flat roof and business signs must follow a uniform code.
naples: Named for Naples in Italy, by promoters who claimed its bay was finer than the original.
It has one of the highest concentrations of millionaires in the United States.
Its pier, built in 1888, has been rebuilt after hurricanes and fires five times.
miami-beach: A barrier island turned into a resort from 1913 by a Quaker farmer who first tried to grow avocados on it.
Its Art Deco district has about 800 buildings from the 1920s and 1930s, the largest such concentration in the world.
Those buildings were saved from demolition in the 1970s by a preservation campaign led by one designer.
everett: Named for the son of an investor, a boy who was eating Everett apples when the question came up.
Boeing’s factory here is the largest building in the world by volume.
It builds the 747, 767, 777 and 787, and has its own fire department and clinics.
spokane: From the Spokane people, whose name means "children of the sun".
It hosted the 1974 World’s Fair, the smallest city ever to do so, and turned its railyards into a riverfront park.
Father’s Day was invented here in 1910 by a woman whose father raised six children alone.
tacoma: From the Lushootseed name for Mount Rainier, Tahoma, meaning "the mother of waters".
Its 1940 suspension bridge, Galloping Gertie, twisted itself apart in the wind four months after opening.
The film of that collapse is shown in engineering courses worldwide.
vancouver: Named for Captain George Vancouver — this is the Washington one, which is older than the Canadian city.
Fort Vancouver here was the headquarters of the Hudson’s Bay Company west of the Rockies.
It sits across the Columbia from Portland, and its residents shop there to avoid sales tax.
eugene: Named for Eugene Skinner, who claimed the land in 1846.
Nike began here when a track coach poured rubber into his wife’s waffle iron to make a sole.
It is called Track Town USA and has hosted the American Olympic trials repeatedly.
boise: From French les bois, "the woods" — trappers seeing trees after crossing the plain.
It has the largest Basque population in the United States, with a whole block devoted to Basque culture.
Its capitol is the only one in the country heated by geothermal water.
ogden: Named for Peter Skene Ogden, a Hudson’s Bay trapper who never settled there.
The transcontinental railroads met at Promontory Summit nearby in 1869, and Ogden became the junction.
Its 25th Street was so rough that Al Capone reportedly called it too wild for him.
salt-lake-city: Named for the Great Salt Lake, the largest lake west of the Mississippi and saltier than the ocean.
Brigham Young led settlers here in 1847 and is said to have declared "this is the right place".
Its streets were laid out wide enough to turn a wagon team around, which is why they are still unusually broad.
fort-collins: Named for a military fort established in 1864 and named for a colonel.
Its Old Town was the model for the Main Street at Disneyland, laid out by a designer who grew up there.
It has more craft breweries per head than almost any American city.
provo: Named for Étienne Provost, a French-Canadian trapper.
Brigham Young University here is the largest religious university in the United States.
It sits between Utah Lake and a mountain wall that rises 2,200 m above the valley floor.
reno: Named for Jesse Reno, a Union general killed in 1862.
It calls itself the Biggest Little City in the World, on an arch that has spanned Virginia Street since 1929.
Nevada’s quick divorces made it the divorce capital of America for decades before Las Vegas took the gambling.
colorado-springs: Named for the Colorado River and for springs in Manitou nearby — the city itself has no springs.
Pikes Peak above it inspired the words to "America the Beautiful" in 1893.
The Air Force Academy and NORAD, dug into Cheyenne Mountain, are both here.
santa-rosa: Named for St Rose of Lima, the first saint born in the Americas.
Luther Burbank bred over 800 plant varieties in his garden here, including the Russet Burbank potato.
Charles Schulz lived in the town, and a Peanuts museum stands near his old ice rink.
stockton: Named for Robert Stockton, a naval commodore in the Mexican-American War.
It was the supply port for the southern goldfields, reached by riverboat from San Francisco.
It became the largest American city ever to declare bankruptcy in 2012, a record since surpassed.
berkeley: Named for George Berkeley, the Irish philosopher, for a line of his about empire moving west.
The university here was the first campus of the University of California, opened in 1868.
The Free Speech Movement began on its steps in 1964, and sixteen chemical elements were discovered in its labs.
modesto: "Modest" — the town was to be named for a banker who declined the honour, so they named it for his modesty.
George Lucas grew up here and based American Graffiti on its cruising culture.
It is the centre of one of the most productive farming counties in the world.
san-mateo: Named for St Matthew, from a Spanish expedition camp in 1776.
It sits in the middle of the San Francisco Peninsula, between the city and Silicon Valley.
Its Coyote Point had one of the first public aviation fields in California.
fresno: Spanish for "ash tree", for the ash growing along the San Joaquin River.
Its county produces more agricultural value than any other in the United States.
It is the nearest large city to Yosemite, Kings Canyon and Sequoia national parks.
bakersfield: Named for Thomas Baker, who grew alfalfa in a field travellers stopped at.
The Bakersfield Sound, a harder-edged country music, was created here by Buck Owens and Merle Haggard.
It sits over one of the largest oilfields in the country, found in 1899.
albuquerque: Named in 1706 for the Duke of Alburquerque, viceroy of New Spain — the first R was dropped later.
Its International Balloon Fiesta is the largest such event in the world, with hundreds of balloons.
A local wind pattern called the box lets balloons return to where they started, which is why it is held here.
riverside: Named simply for its position beside the Santa Ana River.
The navel orange was introduced to America here in 1873 from two Brazilian trees.
One of those original trees is still alive and fenced in a city intersection.
palm-springs: Named for its palm groves and hot springs, which the Cahuilla people used long before it was a resort.
Hollywood stars settled here because studio contracts required them to stay within two hours of Los Angeles.
It has the largest collection of mid-century modern architecture in the world.
glendale: A descriptive name — a glen and a dale, chosen by settlers in 1886; this is the Arizona one.
It sits in the Phoenix metropolitan area and hosts the Cardinals’ stadium.
Its downtown holds one of the largest Christmas light displays in the south-west.
oceanside: Named for its position on the coast, straightforwardly.
Camp Pendleton beside it is one of the largest Marine Corps bases in the country.
Its wooden pier is one of the longest on the West Coast, at about 590 m.
tucson: From the O’odham cuk ṣon, "at the base of the black hill" — the volcanic hill west of the city.
It has been continuously inhabited for about 4,000 years, among the longest of any American city.
It was the first UNESCO City of Gastronomy in the United States, for its desert food traditions.
el-paso: "The pass" — El Paso del Norte, the gap between two mountain ranges that the Rio Grande runs through.
That pass was the main route between Mexico and New Mexico for three centuries.
It forms one binational area with Ciudad Juárez, among the largest on any border in the world.
